QUIET TITLE ACTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105

DECLARATION OF PLAINTIFF'S CLAIMED TITLE AND THE ADVERSE CLAIM CHALLENGED
Jordan Alex Lee ("Plaintiff") states the following regarding real property located at 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, described as Lot 5, Block 12, per map recorded in Book 40, Page 15, San Francisco County Records (the "Property"), also identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, provided for identification only and not as part of the Property's legal description.

Plaintiff's claimed title to the Property, and the basis of that title, is as follows: grant deed recorded January 5, 2020.

Plaintiff seeks a determination of title as of the date of filing.

The following adverse claim(s) to Plaintiff's title are asserted, or may be asserted, by Taylor Morgan, and are the adverse claims against which Plaintiff seeks a determination in this action: an unreleased deed of trust recorded in 1998.

This declaration states Plaintiff's own description of the Property, claimed title, and the adverse claim(s) being challenged; it does not itself determine title to the Property, which is decided by a court in a quiet title action, not by this document.

THE STATUTORY QUIET TITLE ACTION: SCOPE OF THE ACTION
California's Code of Civil Procedure sets out a specific statutory chapter, titled "Quiet Title," governing an action to establish title against adverse claims. That statute states that an action may be brought under this chapter to establish title against adverse claims to real or personal property or any interest therein — a quiet title action is therefore not limited to real property, and is not limited to resolving an uncertain boundary line between adjoining parcels. This is a court proceeding: a lawsuit filed with, and decided by, a court, in contrast to a boundary line agreement (addressed in a separate document in this library), which is a private, out-of-court instrument by which adjoining owners record their own agreement fixing a previously uncertain boundary line without any court's involvement. A quiet title action can be used to resolve a boundary dispute, but it can equally be used to resolve any other adverse claim to title — for example, a dispute over a deed's validity, a lien, an easement's existence or scope, or a claim of adverse possession, which the quiet title statute itself contemplates a plaintiff may rely on as the basis of the title asserted in the action. This clause states only that this statutory cause of action exists and what claims it may address in general terms; it does not evaluate whether a quiet title action is an available or appropriate procedure on the facts of any specific title dispute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) An action may be brought under this chapter to establish title against adverse claims to real or personal property or any interest therein."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 760.020(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, the action's scope (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=760.020.)

The same section's subdivisions (b) and (c), not quoted or relied on in this clause, address a narrow, separate topic (actions to confirm, or challenge, agreements entered into under Public Resources Code sections 6307 or 6357) that has no bearing on the general quiet title action described here and is not addressed anywhere in this document. This clause does not address every procedural prerequisite to filing a quiet title action, such as parties who must be joined, which are addressed, to the extent this document addresses them at all, in other clauses of this same document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on the availability and scope of a quiet title action — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific title dispute; other states' procedures for quieting title, if any, may differ from California's statutory chapter described here.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF A QUIET TITLE COMPLAINT, AND THE VERIFIED-PLEADING REQUIREMENT
California's quiet title statute states specific, mandatory requirements for what a complaint commencing a quiet title action must contain. The complaint must be verified, and must include: (a) a description of the property that is the subject of the action, which, in the case of real property, must include both its legal description and its street address or common designation, if any; (b) the title of the plaintiff as to which a determination is sought and the basis of that title, and, if the title is based on adverse possession, the specific facts constituting the adverse possession; (c) the adverse claims to the plaintiff's title against which a determination is sought; (d) the date as of which the determination is sought, together with a statement of reasons if that date is not the date the complaint is filed; and (e) a prayer for the determination of the plaintiff's title against the adverse claims. The verification requirement is a distinct, and easy to overlook, procedural feature of a quiet title complaint: unlike an ordinary civil complaint, which in most California actions need not be verified, a quiet title complaint must be verified as a matter of this same statute's own text.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The complaint shall be verified and shall include all of the following: (a) A description of the property that is the subject of the action. In the case of tangible personal property, the description shall include its usual location. In the case of real property, the description shall include both its legal description and its street address or common designation, if any. (b) The title of the plaintiff as to which a determination under this chapter is sought and the basis of the title. If the title is based upon adverse possession, the complaint shall allege the specific facts constituting the adverse possession. (c) The adverse claims to the title of the plaintiff against which a determination is sought. (d) The date as of which the determination is sought. If the determination is sought as of a date other than the date the complaint is filed, the complaint shall include a statement of the reasons why a determination as of that date is sought. (e) A prayer for the determination of the title of the plaintiff against the adverse claims."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 761.020, California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, required complaint content and verification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=761.020.)

Proc. section 761.020; they are treated here as one source, not as independent sources. This clause does not address the separate, general statutes governing how a pleading is verified (the form of the affidavit or declaration, and who may make it), which are addressed, to the extent this document addresses them, in a separate clause of this same document. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific complaint's description of the property, statement of title, or statement of adverse claims in fact satisfies this statute, and does not evaluate whether a specific claimant's title is in fact based on adverse possession or any other basis. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's pleading requirements for a quiet title action — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific complaint; other states' pleading requirements for an action to quiet title, if any, may differ from the requirements described here, including on whether verification is required.

COMMENCING THE ACTION AND THE LIS PENDENS RECORDING REQUIREMENT
California's quiet title statute states that an action under this chapter is commenced by filing a complaint with the court, and that immediately upon commencement of the action, the plaintiff must file a notice of the pendency of the action — commonly called a "lis pendens" — in the office of the county recorder of each county in which any real property described in the complaint is located. This recording requirement is a mandatory step tied to the action's commencement, not an optional or later-stage filing. A recorded lis pendens functions as a public record: it gives constructive notice to third parties, such as a prospective purchaser or lender, that title to the described real property is the subject of a pending court action, before that action is resolved.

  "(b) Immediately upon commencement of the action, the plaintiff shall file a notice of the pendency of the action in the office of the county recorder of each county in which any real property described in the complaint is located."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 761.010(b), California Code of Civil Procedure, treated as one source with § 761.010(a) above, not an independent source; the lis pendens recording requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=761.010.)

This clause states the fact that a notice of pendency must be filed, and describes its general constructive-notice function as a public recording; it does not independently research or restate the separate statutory provisions elsewhere in California law that define what a lis pendens must contain, when a claim is a "real property claim" eligible to support one, or how a lis pendens may be expunged, none of which are addressed in this document. This clause does not evaluate whether a lis pendens was in fact properly or timely recorded in any specific action. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's procedure for commencing a quiet title action and its constructive-notice mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific action; other states' procedures for commencing a title action, and their notice-of-pendency mechanisms, if any, may differ from California's.

THE JUDGMENT: NO DEFAULT WITHOUT EVIDENCE OF TITLE, AND ITS BINDING EFFECT
California's quiet title statute departs from the ordinary rule that a defendant's failure to answer a complaint entitles the plaintiff to a default judgment. In a quiet title action, the court must examine into and determine the plaintiff's title against the claims of all the defendants, must not enter judgment by default, and must in all cases require evidence of the plaintiff's title, hearing such evidence as may be offered respecting the claims of any defendant, other than claims whose validity the plaintiff has admitted in the complaint; the court then renders judgment in accordance with the evidence and the law. In other words, a defendant's silence or non-appearance does not by itself establish the plaintiff's title — the statute requires the court to independently examine evidence of title even where no defendant contests the action. Once entered, the statute separately states that the judgment is binding and conclusive, regardless of any legal disability, on all persons known and unknown who were parties to the action and who have any claim to the property, and, subject to a further statutory exception not addressed in this clause, on persons who were not parties to the action but whose claim to the property was not of record at the time the lis pendens (or, if none was filed, the judgment) was recorded.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The court shall examine into and determine the plaintiff’s title against the claims of all the defendants. The court shall not enter judgment by default but shall in all cases require evidence of plaintiff’s title and hear such evidence as may be offered respecting the claims of any of the defendants, other than claims the validity of which is admitted by the plaintiff in the complaint. The court shall render judgment in accordance with the evidence and the law."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 764.010, California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, no default judgment without evidence of title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=764.010.)
  "The judgment in the action is binding and conclusive on all of the following persons, regardless of any legal disability: (a) All persons known and unknown who were parties to the action and who have any claim to the property, whether present or future, vested or contingent, legal or equitable, several or undivided. (b) Except as provided in Section 764.045, all persons who were not parties to the action and who have any claim to the property which was not of record at the time the lis pendens was filed or, if none was filed, at the time the judgment was recorded."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 764.030, California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, binding and conclusive effect of the judgment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=764.030.)

This clause's description of the judgment's binding effect is qualified by an exception stated in section 764.045, which this clause does not independently quote or fully describe, and by section 764.060's separate protection for a purchaser or encumbrancer who relied on the judgment in good faith; a reader should not assume this clause's summary of binding effect is complete without those provisions. This clause states these as general facts about how a California court must proceed and what effect its judgment has; it does not evaluate what evidence would in fact be sufficient to establish any particular plaintiff's title, and does not evaluate the binding effect of any specific judgment on any specific person. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's quiet title judgment procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific title dispute; other states' rules on default judgments and the binding effect of a title judgment, if any, may differ from California's.

NO SINGLE STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS FOR A QUIET TITLE ACTION; IT DEPENDS ON THE UNDERLYING TITLE THEORY
California's quiet title chapter (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 760.010 through 765.060) does not itself state a specific limitations period for filing a quiet title action. Independently of that chapter, California's general statute governing actions to recover real property states that no action for the recovery of real property, or its possession, can be maintained unless the plaintiff, or the plaintiff's ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property within five years before the action is commenced, and a parallel section applies the same five-year period to a cause of action, or defense, arising out of title to real property. Separately, where a plaintiff's claimed title rests on adverse possession — which the quiet title statute itself recognizes as one available basis for a plaintiff's title — California's adverse possession statute requires that the land have been occupied and claimed continuously for five years, with timely payment of taxes levied on the land during that period, before adverse possession is established. Which of these (or other) time periods applies to a given quiet title action depends on the specific legal theory underlying the plaintiff's claimed title and the nature of the adverse claim being challenged, not on a single, uniform statute of limitations that applies to every quiet title action as such.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "No action for the recovery of real property, or for the recovery of the possession thereof, can be maintained, unless it appear that the plaintiff, his ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property in question, within five years before the commencement of the action."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 318, California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year limitations period for an action to recover real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=318.)
  "No cause of action, or defense to an action, arising out of the title to real property, or to rents or profits out of the same, can be effectual, unless it appear that the person prosecuting the action, or making the defense, or under whose title the action is prosecuted, or the defense is made, or the ancestor, predecessor, or grantor of such person was seized or possessed of the premises in question within five years before the commencement of the Act in respect to which such action is prosecuted or defense made."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 319, California Code of Civil Procedure, parallel five-year limitations period for a cause of action or defense arising out of title to real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=319.)
  "In no case shall adverse possession be considered established under the provision of any section of this code, unless it shall be shown that the land has been occupied and claimed for the period of five years continuously, and the party or persons, their predecessors and grantors, have timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes that have been levied and assessed upon the land for the period of five years during which the land has been occupied and claimed."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 325(b), California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year continuous occupation and tax-payment requirement for adverse possession (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=325.)

This clause does not identify a single quiet title-specific limitations statute because independent research in this session, limited to primary statutory sources, did not locate one; whether, and how, a court applies these or other limitations periods (or equitable doctrines such as laches) to a quiet title action asserting a particular theory of title is a question of case law and statutory construction that this clause does not resolve, and a CourtListener search attempted in this research session for case law addressing a quiet title action's limitations period returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day already exhausted, with the next availability reported roughly 9.4 hours out), so no case law is cited or relied on for this clause's statement that no single limitations statute governs every quiet title action. HOW A PLEADING IS VERIFIED: SUBSCRIPTION, AFFIDAVIT CONTENT, AND THE DECLARATION-UNDER-PENALTY-OF-PERJURY ALTERNATIVE
Separately from the quiet title statute's own requirement that a quiet title complaint be verified, California's general pleading statutes state what verifying a pleading requires. Every pleading must be subscribed by the party or the party's attorney, and where a pleading is verified, the affidavit of the party must state that its contents are true of the party's own knowledge, except as to matters stated on information or belief, which the party must state a belief to be true. A separate, general California statute allows an unsworn written statement, declaration, or verification to be used in place of a sworn affidavit for any purpose — including verifying a pleading — if it recites that it is certified or declared to be true under penalty of perjury, is signed, and states the date (and, if executed within California, the place) of execution; that statute sets out suggested language for this purpose, including, for a declaration executed within California, a certification that "the foregoing is true and correct," made under penalty of perjury.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every pleading shall be subscribed by the party or his or her attorney."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 446(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, subscription and affidavit content for a verified pleading (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=446.)
  "such matter may with like force and effect be supported, evidenced, established or proved by the unsworn statement, declaration, verification, or certificate, in writing of such person which recites that it is certified or declared by him or her to be true under penalty of perjury, is subscribed by him or her, and (1), if executed within this state, states the date and place of execution"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2015.5, California Code of Civil Procedure, unsworn declaration under penalty of perjury as an alternative to a sworn affidavit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=2015.5.)

This is one state's general pleading-verification statutes, used as real evidence of how a California pleading may be verified — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific pleading; other states' pleading-verification rules, if any, differ from California's.

I certify (or declare) under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on _________________________ at San Francisco County County, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: _________________________

This verification is a statement made by Plaintiff under penalty of perjury; it is not a notarized acknowledgment, and completing it does not require the involvement of a notary public.

expectedJSON.body: California's quiet title chapter (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 760.010 through 765.060) does not itself state a specific limitations period for filing a quiet title action. Independently of that chapter, California's general statute governing actions to recover real property states that no action for the recovery of real property, or its possession, can be maintained unless the plaintiff, or the plaintiff's ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property within five years before the action is commenced, and a parallel section applies the same five-year period to a cause of action, or defense, arising out of title to real property. Separately, where a plaintiff's claimed title rests on adverse possession — which the quiet title statute itself recognizes as one available basis for a plaintiff's title — California's adverse possession statute requires that the land have been occupied and claimed continuously for five years, with timely payment of taxes levied on the land during that period, before adverse possession is established. Which of these (or other) time periods applies to a given quiet title action depends on the specific legal theory underlying the plaintiff's claimed title and the nature of the adverse claim being challenged, not on a single, uniform statute of limitations that applies to every quiet title action as such.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year limitations period for an action to recover real property
citations.quote: No action for the recovery of real property, or for the recovery of the possession thereof, can be maintained, unless it appear that the plaintiff, his ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property in question, within five years before the commencement of the action.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, parallel five-year limitations period for a cause of action or defense arising out of title to real property
citations.quote: No cause of action, or defense to an action, arising out of the title to real property, or to rents or profits out of the same, can be effectual, unless it appear that the person prosecuting the action, or making the defense, or under whose title the action is prosecuted, or the defense is made, or the ancestor, predecessor, or grantor of such person was seized or possessed of the premises in question within five years before the commencement of the Act in respect to which such action is prosecuted or defense made.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year continuous occupation and tax-payment requirement for adverse possession
citations.quote: In no case shall adverse possession be considered established under the provision of any section of this code, unless it shall be shown that the land has been occupied and claimed for the period of five years continuously, and the party or persons, their predecessors and grantors, have timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes that have been levied and assessed upon the land for the period of five years during which the land has been occupied and claimed.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the quiet title statute's own requirement that a quiet title complaint be verified, California's general pleading statutes state what verifying a pleading requires. Every pleading must be subscribed by the party or the party's attorney, and where a pleading is verified, the affidavit of the party must state that its contents are true of the party's own knowledge, except as to matters stated on information or belief, which the party must state a belief to be true. A separate, general California statute allows an unsworn written statement, declaration, or verification to be used in place of a sworn affidavit for any purpose — including verifying a pleading — if it recites that it is certified or declared to be true under penalty of perjury, is signed, and states the date (and, if executed within California, the place) of execution; that statute sets out suggested language for this purpose, including, for a declaration executed within California, a certification that "the foregoing is true and correct," made under penalty of perjury.
